title: Development of Family-Centred Maternity Care and History of Modern Medical Services and Midwifery in Nigeria
introduction: Family-centred maternity care evolved as a humane reaction against rigid hospital isolation rules that separated mothers, fathers, and newborns during childbirth. In Nigeria, the evolution of modern medical services and formal midwifery grew out of early missionary hospitals, colonial health policies, post-war educational expansion, and pioneering Nigerian registered midwives.
learningOutcomes: 2.1 Define Family-Centred Care (FCC), state its five core principles and clinical benefits, and trace how rigid hospital practices triggered the 1940 reform movement.
2.2 Explain the three key concepts that shaped family-centred maternity care: natural childbirth, Gesell's rooming-in, and Bowlby's maternal deprivation.

2.3 Trace the introduction and growth of Western medicine in Nigeria from missionary establishments (1860s) through British colonial services, World Wars I and II, and the 1946 Ten-Year Health Development Plan.
2.4 Compare the distribution and ownership of Nigerian health facilities across federal, state, local government, and private sectors in the late 20th century.
2.5 Outline key milestones in the history and professional training of midwifery in Nigeria, including pioneering registered midwives and the 1930 Midwife Ordinance.

content.heading: Concept, Principles, and Benefits of Family-Centred Care (FCC)
content.body: Family-centred care (FCC)—frequently used interchangeably with patient-centered care—is a partnership approach to health care decision-making in which families are recognized as partners, collaborators, and experts in the care delivery process. FCC rests on five core principles: (1) Information Sharing—open, objective, and unbiased exchange of clinical information; (2) Respect and Honoring Differences—valuing diversity, cultural and linguistic traditions, and individual care preferences; (3) Partnership and Collaboration—jointly making medically appropriate decisions tailored to family needs, strengths, values, and abilities at the family's chosen level of participation; (4) Negotiation—maintaining flexible rather than rigid medical care plans; and (5) Care in Context of Family and Community—aligning direct medical care with the child's home, school, daily activities, and community quality of life. Implementing FCC yields three documented benefits: it increases patient health, increases family and patient satisfaction, and improves overall health care quality.

content.heading: Evolution of Family-Centred Maternity Care and Its Three Core Concepts
content.body: The need to train indigenous health care manpower was recognized early—first by Christian missionaries (who suffered high morbidity and mortality from inclement weather and unfamiliar tropical diseases while using health care as part of hinterland evangelism) and later by the colonial government. Missionaries sponsored Africans to train in Britain, contributing to rising hospital deliveries. However, as childbirth moved into hospitals under early germ theory, rules became highly rigid: maternity patients were isolated, partners were separated during labour and delivery, mothers and newborns were separated immediately after birth, and rigid formula-feeding schedules with strict asepsis replaced natural bonding. The turning point came in 1940 when parents resisted these rigid rules while social scientists documented the psychological necessity of maternal bonding for child development and emotional security. This reform generated three landmark concepts: (1) Natural Childbirth—providing expectant mothers with antenatal classes on normal pregnancy, labour, and relaxation exercises while ensuring the husband or a trusted support person remains present for reassurance; (2) Rooming-In—introduced by Arnold Gesell, keeping newborns with their mothers rather than removing them to separate nurseries so both mother and father adjust to caring for the infant; and (3) Maternal Deprivation—described by John Bowlby (Prowlby), whose research on the adverse mental-health effects of separating mother and child cemented personalized, comprehensive, family-centred care.

content.heading: Missionary and Colonial Origins of Modern Medical Services in Nigeria
content.body: Western medicine was formally introduced into Nigeria in the 1860s when Roman Catholic missionaries established Sacred Heart Hospital in Abeokuta. Throughout the colonial era, religious missions supplied a huge proportion of modern facilities: Roman Catholic missions predominated (accounting for roughly 40% of mission hospital beds by 1960, heavily concentrated in the south-eastern and mid-western regions, where they ran almost all hospitals by 1954). By 1960, mission hospitals slightly outnumbered government hospitals (118 mission vs. 101 government). In the middle belt and Islamic north, the Sudan United Mission and Sudan Interior Mission respectively operated 25 hospitals and facilities that remained vital into 1990. Missions also trained nurses and paramedical staff, sponsored the first generation of Western-educated Nigerian doctors abroad, and built general education that promoted acceptance of modern medicine. Meanwhile, the British colonial government began building clinics and hospitals in Lagos, Calabar, and coastal trading centres in the 1870s—initially strictly for Europeans before gradually extending services to African employees of European enterprises.

content.heading: World Wars, the 1946 Health Plan, and Health System Expansion
content.body: World War I severely disrupted Nigerian medical services as large numbers of European and African medical personnel were pulled away to serve in Europe; post-war recovery brought expanded facilities and government schools training Nigerian medical assistants. However, discriminatory colonial rules prohibited even European-trained Nigerian physicians from practising in government hospitals unless treating African patients—fueling protests and bringing medical personnel into nationalist movements. Partly in response to nationalist agitation after World War II, the colonial administration launched the 1946 Ten-Year Health Development Plan, establishing the Ministry of Health to coordinate government, private, and mission services, though funding heavily favoured urban cities and southern regions over rural and northern areas. The University of Ibadan was founded in 1948 with Nigeria's first full Faculty of Medicine and University College Hospital (UCH); alongside two pharmacy schools, government nursing and midwifery schools grew to 65 by 1960. By 1979, Nigeria had 562 general hospitals, 16 maternity/paediatric hospitals, 11 armed forces hospitals, 6 teaching hospitals, and 3 prison hospitals (totalling ~44,600 beds), plus nearly 600 general health centres, 2,740 clinics, 930 maternity homes, and 1,240 maternal health centres. By 1985, ownership spanned 84 federal establishments (13% of beds), 3,023 state establishments (47% of beds), 6,331 local government establishments (11% of beds), and 1,436 private establishments (14% of beds).

content.heading: History and Professional Development of Midwifery in Nigeria
content.body: Maternal and newborn care in Nigeria historically lagged behind developed nations primarily due to inadequate human and material resources (doctors, midwives, hospitals, health centres, and maternity homes). Following the global pattern, traditional older women in the family initially assisted births until missionaries trained young Nigerian women as auxiliaries. In 1912, the first two Nigerian registered midwives trained abroad—the late Mrs. Ore Green and Mrs. Abimbola Gibson—followed by Mrs. Peregrino, Mrs. Franklin, and Mrs. Adebisi, who were designated state certified midwives. In July 1927, Miss Josephine Durojaiye became the first Nigerian-trained registered midwife, qualifying at African Hospital, Ijebu-Ode (now General Hospital, Ijebu-Ode). From 1928, local training expanded, and in 1930 the first Midwife Ordinance was enacted and published on 1st April 1931. Midwives trained at Massey Street, Lagos were classified as Grade I midwives, while those trained outside Lagos were Grade II until that tier was abolished in 1968 (when Iyienu Hospital, Anambra also began training Grade I midwives). Over time, training durations shifted between 3-year basic and 18-month or 1-year post-basic programmes; the basic midwifery programme was later recommenced to curb rising maternal mortality, midwifery was also integrated into university BNSc programmes (with graduates sitting the council examination), and 62 post-basic midwifery schools produce Registered Midwives (R.M.) holding three-yearly renewable practising licences.

inTextQuestions.question: Who first recognized the need for indigenous health manpower training in Nigeria, and why?
inTextQuestions.answer: First the missionaries and later the colonial government, primarily because missionary physicians suffered high morbidity and mortality from inclement weather and unfamiliar tropical diseases while expanding services into the hinterland.

inTextQuestions.question: Where and by whom was the first Western hospital in Nigeria established in the 1860s?
inTextQuestions.answer: Sacred Heart Hospital in Abeokuta, established by Roman Catholic missionaries.

inTextQuestions.question: Who introduced the concept of 'rooming-in', and what does it mean?
inTextQuestions.answer: Arnold Gesell introduced rooming-in, which means newborn infants stay with their mothers after birth instead of being separated into a nursery, enabling both parents to bond with and care for the infant.

inTextQuestions.question: Who was the first Nigerian-trained registered midwife, and where and when did she qualify?
inTextQuestions.answer: Miss Josephine Durojaiye, who qualified in July 1927 at the African Hospital, Ijebu-Ode (now General Hospital, Ijebu-Ode).

saqs.question: Define Family-Centred Care (FCC), list its five core principles, and state its three primary benefits.
saqs.answer: Family-Centred Care is a partnership approach to health care decision-making that treats families as partners, collaborators, and experts in care delivery. Its five principles are: (1) Information Sharing, (2) Respect and Honoring Differences, (3) Partnership and Collaboration, (4) Negotiation, and (5) Care in Context of Family and Community. Its three benefits are increased patient health, increased satisfaction, and higher health care quality.

saqs.question: Explain why 1940 was a turning point in maternity care and define natural childbirth, rooming-in, and maternal deprivation.
saqs.answer: In 1940, parents and social scientists resisted rigid hospital germ-theory rules that isolated mothers, excluded fathers, and separated newborns. This prompted three concepts: Natural Childbirth (antenatal preparation, relaxation, and partner support during labour), Rooming-In (Arnold Gesell's practice of keeping newborns with their mothers rather than in nurseries), and Maternal Deprivation (John Bowlby's demonstration of the harmful developmental and mental-health effects of mother-infant separation).

saqs.question: Outline the major milestones in Nigeria's modern medical history between 1860 and 1960, including the roles of missions and the 1946 health plan.
saqs.answer: Roman Catholic missionaries introduced Western medicine in the 1860s with Sacred Heart Hospital in Abeokuta, later joined by Sudan United and Sudan Interior Missions in the Middle Belt and North; missions trained nurses and sponsored early Nigerian doctors, operating 118 hospitals by 1960 versus 101 government hospitals. British colonial hospitals began in Lagos and Calabar in the 1870s (initially for Europeans). Following WWII and nationalist protests, the 1946 Ten-Year Health Development Plan established the Ministry of Health, the University of Ibadan and UCH were founded in 1948, and 65 government nursing/midwifery schools operated by 1960.

saqs.question: Trace the early milestones of registered midwifery in Nigeria from 1912 to 1968.
saqs.answer: In 1912, late Mrs. Ore Green and Mrs. Abimbola Gibson became the first two Nigerian registered midwives trained abroad (followed by Mrs. Peregrino, Mrs. Franklin, and Mrs. Adebisi). In July 1927, Miss Josephine Durojaiye became the first Nigerian-trained registered midwife at African Hospital, Ijebu-Ode. In 1930, the first Midwife Ordinance was enacted (published 1st April 1931). Massey Street Lagos trained Grade I midwives while schools outside Lagos trained Grade II midwives until Grade II was abolished in 1968.

saqs.question: Why has maternal and newborn care historically lagged in Nigeria compared to developed countries, and what training pathways exist for Nigerian midwives?
saqs.answer: Care has lagged largely due to inadequate human and material resources—insufficient doctors, midwives, hospitals, health centres, and maternity homes. Training pathways include recommenced 3-year basic midwifery programmes (to curb maternal mortality), 18-month post-basic midwifery programmes across accredited schools, and midwifery integrated into university BNSc programmes leading to the Council qualifying examination and 3-yearly renewable R.M. practising licences.
